explanations.explanation: Hats go on heads, I run my whole kitchen on that rule, so I get the guess. But John says, "There were ten royal crowns on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads." The crowns sit on the horns. The heads carry the blasphemous names.

You caught the placement, baker. John says, "There were ten royal crowns on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads." So the crowns go on the horns, and the heads carry the names. This beast has a very strange idea of where accessories belong.

That's the one. John says, "And the dragon gave the beast his power and his throne and great authority." The dragon is the devil and Satan (Revelation 12:9). So whatever this beast has, it got handed to it.

Michael is the angel who fought the dragon (Revelation 12:7), so he's on the other side of this story. John says the one who gave the beast its power, throne and authority was the dragon. Michael shows up in the chapter before, and that's probably why his name popped into your head.

The crowns on the beast's horns make kings a fair guess. But the text names the giver: "the dragon gave the beast his power and his throne and great authority." The kings aren't mentioned as the source here. The dragon is.
Right on the money. John says one head "appeared to have been mortally wounded. But the mortal wound was healed." That's the turn in the verse. The wound was deadly, and then it was healed.

Spreading would make this a sadder story for the beast, but that's not what John sees. He says, "the mortal wound was healed." The wound goes away instead of growing. Hold onto that word, because the whole world reacts to it.
Hidden is a sneaky guess, like covering a burnt cookie with extra sprinkles. But John doesn't say the wound was covered up. He says, "the mortal wound was healed." It's healed, not hidden.

You've got it. John says, "the mortal wound was healed, and the whole world marveled and followed the beast." The healing is what gets everyone's attention. The whole world marvels, and then it follows.

The text says the opposite. John writes, "the mortal wound was healed, and the whole world marveled and followed the beast." So the healing makes the whole world marvel, and the world follows. Nobody turns away in this verse.

It sounds like the crowd might only care about the beast, but John says more. "They worshiped the dragon who had given authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast." So the dragon gets worship too. The crowd gives it to both.

Good catch, baker. John says, "They worshiped the dragon who had given authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast." So the crowd worships both the dragon and the beast. Never is a strong word, and the text proves it isn't true here.

That's how the crowd's words come across. They ask, "Who is like the beast, and who can wage war against it?" It's a question with an answer already built in: nobody. And these are the people who just watched the wound get healed.

explanations.answer: It will lose a war soon
explanations.explanation: That would be quite the plot twist, but the crowd isn't saying that. They ask, "Who is like the beast, and who can wage war against it?" That's a boast, and they sound sure of themselves. Nothing about it hints at losing.

I can see how "who can wage war" sounds like a call to arms. But the crowd is worshiping the beast when they say it (Revelation 13:4). I think they're saying nobody could take it on. They aren't asking for a volunteer.
You've got it. The beast was given "authority to act for 42 months." Notice the words "was given" again. Whatever it does has a limit placed on it.
Twelve months is one year, and that's a nice tidy number. But the verse says "authority to act for 42 months." It's not 12, so check the number twice, baker. Forty-two is the one.
Seventy is a nice round number, and I understand why it feels right. But John says "authority to act for 42 months." That's the number in the verse. The time is given, and it's 42.
That's it. John says the beast opened its mouth "to speak blasphemies against God and to slander His name and His tabernacle." It's a hard thing to hear. The words are aimed straight at God.

The dragon is the one who gave the beast its power (Revelation 13:2), so this guess makes sense. But the beast doesn't turn on him. John says it speaks "blasphemies against God." The people even worship the dragon along with the beast (Revelation 13:4).

The nations do come up in the next verse, where the beast is given authority over every tribe and people and tongue and nation (Revelation 13:7). But that's authority, not blasphemy. The blasphemies in verse 6 are "against God and to slander His name."

explanations.answer: Every tribe and nation on earth
explanations.explanation: That's right, and it's a big reach. John says the beast "was given authority over every tribe and people and tongue and nation." This is a heavy verse. It names every tribe, people, tongue and nation.

explanations.answer: The kings along the shore of the sea
explanations.explanation: The beast rises out of the sea, so a shoreline guess is understandable. But the text doesn't limit it to a coast or a handful of kings. John says the authority covers "every tribe and people and tongue and nation." It's far wider than the shore.

explanations.answer: The rulers of one great nation
explanations.explanation: One nation would be a much smaller reach, but that's not what the verse says. John says authority was given "over every tribe and people and tongue and nation." It isn't one nation. It's all of them, and that's a heavy thing.
That's the name. John says it's "the Book of Life belonging to the Lamb who was slain." The names in it were written "from the foundation of the world." The Lamb is Jesus (John 1:29).

The Book of the Law is a real book in Scripture. Joshua, Moses' successor as Israel's leader, was told about it (Joshua 1:8). But it isn't the book John names here. This one is "the Book of Life belonging to the Lamb who was slain."

The Book of Jashar is a real book, and Joshua 10:13 mentions it. It's a more obscure choice than most, baker. But John names a different book here, "the Book of Life belonging to the Lamb who was slain."

explanations.answer: The saints to persevere in faith
explanations.explanation: That's what John says. After the hard word about captivity and the sword, he writes, "Here is a call for the perseverance and faith of the saints." It's a heavy part of the passage. The call is to keep going, with faith.

explanations.answer: The saints to strike back at the beast
explanations.explanation: I can see why a call after this much trouble might sound like a call to fight. But John doesn't say that. He says, "Here is a call for the perseverance and faith of the saints." The call is for perseverance and faith.

explanations.answer: The saints to flee into the wilderness
explanations.explanation: Running away is a natural guess when things get this hard. But this verse doesn't send anyone to the wilderness. John says, "Here is a call for the perseverance and faith of the saints." So the call is for perseverance and faith.
Yes, that's the twist. This beast "had two horns like a lamb, but spoke like a dragon." It looks one way and sounds another. Never judge a cookie by how it looks in the box, baker.

A lamb and a shepherd go together nicely, which is probably why this one tempted you. But the verse says the beast "had two horns like a lamb, but spoke like a dragon." Nothing here says it sounds like a shepherd. The voice is a dragon's.

A dove is the shape of Minty, one of my cookie cutter kids, so I know a gentle bird when I see one. This beast isn't gentle where it counts. John says it "had two horns like a lamb, but spoke like a dragon." The voice doesn't match the look.
You've got it. John says the second beast "caused the earth and those who dwell in it to worship the first beast." It's also using all the first beast's authority. It works for the first beast.

The text says the opposite. John says the second beast "caused the earth and those who dwell in it to worship the first beast, whose mortal wound had been healed." So it does get the earth to worship the first beast. It sends the worship in that direction.
That's the word. John says, "it deceived those who dwell on the earth." The signs it was given to perform are what it uses. The signs were real enough to fool people.

Healing was last verse's story, when the first beast's wound was healed (Revelation 13:3), so I see the mix-up. But the second beast doesn't heal the people. John says the signs let it deceive "those who dwell on the earth."

Warning would mean the people got fair notice, and that isn't what happens. John says the beast "deceived those who dwell on the earth." The signs it performed on behalf of the first beast led to deception. So deceives is the word.

Right. John says the beast deceived people "telling them to make an image to the beast that had been wounded by the sword and yet had lived." The people are told to build it. Then it gets breath (Revelation 13:15).
A temple would make sense for worship, but John doesn't say the people build one. The second beast tells them to "make an image to the beast." The word in the verse is image.

Crowns already show up on the first beast's horns (Revelation 13:1), so that one might have stuck in your head. But the second beast tells the people to "make an image to the beast." Nobody is told to make a crown here. The thing to make is an image.

That's the word. The second beast "was permitted to give breath to the image of the first beast, so that the image could speak." Notice "permitted" again. That's a gift handed over, not power the beast owns on its own.

Gold feels natural for an image, and you might picture something shiny. But the verse says the beast was permitted to give "breath to the image of the first beast." The image speaks because of that breath. The verse doesn't mention gold.

Wings would be quite the upgrade for an image, I'll give you that. But the verse says the second beast was permitted to give "breath to the image of the first beast." With breath, the image can speak. That's what the verse gives it.
That's right. John says the mark goes "on their right hand or on their forehead." Those are the two places named. The second beast requires it of "all people."
The right side is the right start, but the ear and foot aren't in the verse. John says the mark goes "on their right hand or on their forehead." Those are the two places the text names.
Hands and a body spot are in the right area, so I see why this felt close. But John says the mark is "on their right hand or on their forehead." The verse says right hand, and chest isn't mentioned.

explanations.answer: No one could buy or sell without it
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives. The mark is required "so that no one could buy or sell unless he had the mark." Without it, no buying and no selling. It touches everyday life.

explanations.answer: No one could marry or own land without it
explanations.explanation: Marriage and land are big parts of life, but the verse doesn't list them. John says the mark is required "so that no one could buy or sell unless he had the mark." The text talks about buying and selling.

explanations.answer: No one could enter a city without it
explanations.explanation: Gates and cities are a fair guess for a rule like this. But the text doesn't mention cities at all. The mark is required "so that no one could buy or sell unless he had the mark."

I see why the dragon came to mind, since he's the one who gave the first beast its power (Revelation 13:2). But the mark isn't his name. John says it's "the name of the beast or the number of its name." The beast is the one named.

You caught it. John says no one could buy or sell "unless he had the mark, the name of the beast or the number of its name." The mark is tied to the beast's name or the number of its name. The dragon's name isn't in the verse.

You've got it. John says, "for it is the number of a man, and that number is 666." He opens with, "Here is a call for wisdom," so the number comes with a call to think. That's a good place to end the passage.
That number doesn't show up in this passage, so this one is a swing and a miss at the number. John says the number of the beast "is the number of a man, and that number is 666." The answer is 666.
Three sevens in a row look tidy, and I understand the pull. But John says "the number of a man, and that number is 666." Three sevens aren't what the verse says. It's 666.
